subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Saurabh, you're doing that thing I used to do. Nodding when you don't understand. I can see it from here.
Let me tell you something. When I was a girl of twenty-four, new in the accounts department of the old textile mill, I heard the word 'reconciliation' fifty times in my first week. I had no idea what it meant. I wrote it on my palm to look up at home. I was sure if I asked, they'd send me back.
One afternoon Mr Kulkarni handed me a file and said, 'Sonali, reconcile this.' I stood there. Then I said, 'Sir, I'm sorry. What does reconcile mean here, exactly?'
He didn't laugh. He pulled up a chair, showed me two ledgers, and said, 'You match these, line by line. That's all.' Then he went back to his tea.
That's all, Saurabh. Nobody laughed. So, what is it you want to ask?

qa.q: Where did Sonali write the word 'reconciliation' to look it up at home?
qa.a: She wrote it on her palm.

qa.q: What was Sonali afraid would happen if she asked Mr Kulkarni?
qa.a: She was afraid of being humiliated and even of being sent back for not knowing.

qa.q: What is Sonali encouraging Saurabh to do?
qa.a: She is inviting Saurabh to ask the question openly, since asking basic things is normal and usually gets a plain, kind answer.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel hearing that Mr Kulkarni didn't laugh?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel relief and less fear about asking, seeing that the humiliation Saurabh dreads may never come.

grounding: It shows a young employee asking a basic question, getting a kind, matter-of-fact reply, and the fear of hiding ignorance starting to loosen.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
The front page closed at 11:20, and it was 11:02 when the night editor dropped a story on Nikita's desk. 'Needs a kicker. Quick.'
Nikita, three weeks at the newspaper, had heard 'kicker' a dozen times. She had nodded every time.
She searched her notes. Nothing. The clock over the news desk ticked. She thought of guessing, of writing anything and hoping.
Gautam, the chief sub-editor, was at the next desk, headphones on, fixing a headline. Her heart was banging.
She tapped his shoulder. 'Sorry, basic question. What exactly is a kicker?'
He slid one headphone off. 'The small line above the headline. Two or three words. Sets the tone. Like "Monsoon woes".' He put the headphone back.
That was it. No sigh. No look.
Nikita wrote the kicker in two minutes. At 11:18 she sent the page. Her hands had stopped shaking.

qa.q: What time did the front page close?
What was Nikita afraid of before she tapped Gautam's shoulder?
qa.a: She was afraid of looking foolish for not knowing a word she had heard a dozen times and nodded at.

qa.q: What did Nikita's choice to ask show her about asking basic questions?
qa.a: It showed that a quick, honest question gets a plain answer and saves time, while hiding would have meant guessing under deadline.

qa.q: How does Gautam seem to see Nikita's question?
qa.a: He treats it as an ordinary work question, answering briefly and going back to his headline without judgement.

grounding: It shows a new journalist under deadline asking a basic question and getting a kind, matter-of-fact reply, so the fear of exposing ignorance loosens.
